summary: Mike Padlipsky replies to RFC 514 and RFC 519, which disagree about network information: one finds too many requests for it, the other says newcomers find it hard to learn about hosts. He tries to resolve the feast-or-famine puzzle. It is a commentary.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 531 responds to complaints that people ask for too much network information while newcomers cannot find enough. The author argues that the Resource Notebook is a useful starting point, if people use it and improve it.

subtitle: A reply to two different complaints about finding and providing network information.

tldr.problem: RFC 514 describes too many requests for host information, while RFC 519 says newcomers struggle to learn how to use network hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Padlipsky argues that the Resource Notebook already offers host details, technical liaison contacts and references, and should be treated as the primary source of host information.
tldr.outcome: The author says the Notebook needs better content and wider distribution. It should help users find their way, but does not replace each host's manual.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 531's status as Unknown and names no RFC that updates or replaces it. The RFC is a response to RFC 514 and RFC 519.

sections.title: Two Complaints About Information
sections.content:
Padlipsky compares two recent concerns. RFC 514 says people spend too much time asking for information about network hosts. RFC 519 says it is not easy to learn how to use those hosts. This can look like both too much and too little information at once.

He notes that large servers can face a heavy burden from requests. He gives Multics as an example, with about 50 cubic feet of system listings as well as many user-supplied programs.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network staff received many requests for information. At the same time, newcomers said they could not find the information they needed.

sections.title: The Resource Notebook
sections.content:
The author argues that useful information already exists in the Resource Notebook, but people are not using it. The Notebook lists technical liaisons, describes hosts that may interest network users and points to other published information. Its Multics section offers a programmers' manual to any network site that requests one.

Padlipsky says the Notebook could have helped investigators who struggled to log in and could have directed broad requests for host information to people able to answer them.
sections.plainLanguage: The Resource Notebook lists host information, contact people and other sources. The author says users who consult it could get help before sending broad requests or making repeated login attempts.

sections.title: How the Notebook Should Be Used
sections.content:
Padlipsky does not present the Notebook as a complete solution. He says it needs stronger content and wider distribution, and notes that an online users' packet or microfiche could help people find it. The Notebook is not a replacement for individual host manuals, though it can hold documentation for commands that apply generally.

He asks the Network Working Group to treat the Resource Notebook as the primary source of host information and to improve it rather than assume that no information is available.
sections.plainLanguage: The Notebook is incomplete, and each host still needs its own manual. The author wants people to use the Notebook first and help improve it.
